title: Rome, unhindered (Acts 28:30–31)
hook: Paul under house arrest, welcoming all, preaching with confidence

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shipwreck, and every soul brought safe to Malta. Your line was not a hair shall perish. Were you the calm one for someone? Day five hundred fifty-eight.

On day five hundred thirty-four, at the very start of Acts, Jesus told his friends they would be his witnesses in Jerusalem, in Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. Since then we've followed the story out of the upper room, through Samaria and the desert road, to Antioch, across the sea to Philippi, Athens and Corinth, and through a shipwreck. Today it arrives in the capital of the world as Luke's readers knew it. And Paul walks into Rome as a prisoner.
screen: `JERUSALEM, JUDEA, SAMARIA.` → `ANTIOCH, PHILIPPI, ATHENS.` → `AND NOW, ROME.`

segments.voice: As Paul nears the city on the Appian Way, believers from Rome walk out to meet him, at the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns. Luke says that when Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage. Even an apostle needed friends to show up. In Rome he's allowed to live by himself, with a soldier guarding him. He calls together the leaders of the Jewish community and speaks with them all day, from morning to evening. Some are persuaded, some are not, and they leave still discussing among themselves. Then come the last two verses of the book. In the King James: "And Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house, and received all that came in unto him, Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching those things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, no man forbidding him." That's how Acts ends. Not with Paul's trial. Not with his death. The last word in the Greek is akolutos: unhindered, without hindrance. A man in chains, renting a room, opening his door to whoever comes, and the word is not chained. Why does Luke stop there? Nobody knows for certain. Maybe he wrote before the trial ended. Maybe he wanted the story to stay open, because it isn't finished. Catholic tradition holds that Paul was later martyred in Rome under Nero, beheaded, and buried on the road to Ostia, where the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls now stands. The Church keeps his feast with Peter's on June twenty-ninth.
screen: `FRIENDS WALK OUT TO MEET HIM.` · `A ROOM, A GUARD, AN OPEN DOOR.` · `HE RECEIVED ALL THAT CAME.` · `THE BOOK ENDS OPEN.` · then, large: `WITHOUT HINDRANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome whoever comes. Settle, and breathe. Paul couldn't go anywhere, so he let the world come to him. Picture your own small room today: your desk, your kitchen, your phone. Who might come through it? An unexpected call, a neighbor, a coworker with a question, a kid with a long story. Decide now to receive them, the way Paul received all that came in. Not grudgingly. With the door open. If you pray, you can thank God for the friends who walked out to meet you when you needed it. The bell holds the time.
Rome. Where Acts ends, with Paul in a rented room, welcoming everyone, preaching without hindrance. Today's word.

Your line: without hindrance. Today, open your door to whoever comes. And that's the Acts of the Apostles: witnesses, Pentecost, deacons, the road to Damascus, the council, Lydia, the jail, Athens, the shipwreck, and Rome. Tomorrow, the letters. Day five hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate Saints Peter and Paul together on June 29, and pilgrims to Rome visit Paul's tomb at the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls, on the road to Ostia.

original.note: Greek: unhindered, without hindrance. the very last word of the Acts of the Apostles.

trapdoor: what you thought: Acts ends with Paul's death in Rome.
what it means: it ends with a prisoner in a rented room, welcoming all, preaching freely: the story left open.
what a scholar hears: the last word is akōlytōs, unhindered. Paul's martyrdom under Nero comes from early tradition, such as Clement of Rome and later writers, not from Acts.

notes: Akōlytōs as the final word of Acts: standard; confirm.
